questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Outline the common characteristics of:

(i) Echinoids; (4 marks)
(ii) Bivalves; (4 marks)
(iii) Gastropods. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Echinoids, the sea urchins (phylum Echinodermata, class Echinoidea) (4 marks)**

- Marine, mostly bottom-living (benthic) animals; range from the **Ordovician to the Recent**, common in the Jurassic and Cretaceous.
- The skeleton is a rigid, hollow, **globular, heart-shaped or flattened (disc) "test"** made of **calcite plates** that are firmly fitted together (they have no hinge); in life it is covered by movable **spines** on small bumps (**tubercles**), which are usually lost after death.
- The test is built of **five double rows of ambulacral plates** (with **pairs of pores** for the tube feet) which alternate with **five double rows of interambulacral plates**, so there is **pentamerous (five-fold) radial symmetry**; in regular urchins the mouth (peristome) is underneath and the anus (periproct) is at the top, while in **irregular urchins** the anus has moved to the side or base and the symmetry has become bilateral.
- An **apical system** (with the madreporite) at the top; the mouth contains the chewing apparatus (**Aristotle's lantern**); the plates are made of single crystals of calcite with a porous (stereom) structure. Examples: *Micraster*, *Echinocorys*, *Cidaris*.

**(ii) Bivalves (phylum Mollusca, class Bivalvia, formerly Lamellibranchia) (4 marks)**

- Marine and freshwater animals, living on the bottom, in burrows, attached to rocks or swimming; range from the **Cambrian to the Recent**.
- The shell has **two valves** (left and right), usually **mirror images of each other** (equivalve), so that the plane of symmetry **lies between the valves**; each valve is normally asymmetrical, with the **umbo (beak)**, the oldest part, towards the hinge, and shows **concentric growth lines**.
- The valves are joined at the **hinge** by an elastic **ligament** and by **teeth and sockets**, and they are closed by **adductor muscles**, whose scars and the **pallial line** (with the pallial sinus in burrowers) are visible inside the valve.
- The shell is made of calcite or aragonite with no head; many have ribs, spines or ridges. Examples: *Gryphaea*, *Pecten*, *Ostrea*, *Inoceramus*, *Trigonia*.

**(iii) Gastropods (phylum Mollusca, class Gastropoda) (4 marks)**

- Marine, freshwater and land animals (snails, whelks, limpets, slugs); range from the **Cambrian to the Recent**.
- The shell is a **single piece (univalve)**, usually **coiled in a spiral (helicospiral) and asymmetrical**, although some are cap-shaped (limpets) or coiled in one plane (planispiral); the tube widens to an **aperture** from which the head and foot emerge.
- It consists of **whorls** which join at the **suture**, forming a **spire** with an **apex** (the oldest, first whorl) and a **columella** at the centre; there may be an **umbilicus**, and a **siphonal notch or canal** at the aperture in carnivorous marine forms, and growth lines and ornament (ribs, spines, knobs).
- Most coil clockwise (dextral). Examples: *Turritella*, *Natica*, *Murex*, *Planorbis*, *Cerithium*.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Discuss the following methods of relative dating and outline their limitations:

(i) Tree ring dating;
(ii) Varved clay dating.

(13 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Both methods rely on **annual layers** which can be counted back from a known recent date, so they give ages in years; they are often treated, as in this question, with the "relative" methods because they cover only the recent past and are based on counting and correlating layers rather than on radioactive decay.

**(i) Tree ring dating (dendrochronology) (about 6 to 7 marks)**

*Method.* In temperate regions, a tree adds **one growth ring each year** to its trunk: light-coloured, wide **earlywood** (spring) and dark, dense **latewood** (summer to autumn) make one ring. Wet, warm years give wide rings, dry or cold years give narrow rings. The rings of a section or of a core of wood are **counted** back from the outer ring (the year of felling), and the **pattern of wide and narrow rings** is **cross-dated** (matched) with the patterns of other trees, living and dead (old beams, buried or sub-fossil wood), so that an overlapping **master chronology** reaching back several thousand years (about 10 000 years in the best records) is built. It is used to date **recent geological events** (landslides, floods, volcanic eruptions, glacier advances, fault movements, shifts of dunes), archaeological timbers, **past climate**, and to calibrate radiocarbon ages.

*Limitations.*

- Only trees from climates with a **marked seasonal cycle** form clear annual rings; in **equatorial rain forests** with no strong season (for example much of southern Cameroon), rings are indistinct or absent.
- **False rings (two in one year) or missing rings** (in drought, fire, insect attack) give errors and need careful cross-dating.
- It covers only the **last 10 000 years or so**, and only where **old wood has been preserved** in an overlapping sequence; it cannot be used for older rocks.
- The records are **regional** (they depend on species and local climate), a tree responds to local conditions as well as climate, and **sampling is limited** (coring damages the tree; the trunk may be rotten at the centre).

**(ii) Varved clay dating (geochronology) (about 6 to 7 marks)**

*Method.* A **varve** is a **pair of annual layers in a lake sediment**, typical of **glacial lakes** at the edge of an ice sheet. In summer, melt-water brings in plenty of sediment, so a **thick, light-coloured, coarser layer of silt and fine sand** is deposited; in winter, the lake freezes, the water is still, and only the finest material and organic matter settles to give a **thin, dark layer of clay**. Each couplet equals **one year**, so counting varves gives the number of years of deposition, and by matching thick and thin couplets from lake to lake (as the Swede Gerard De Geer did in Sweden) a continuous **varve chronology** of about 13 000 years is produced. It is used to date the **retreat of ice sheets** at the end of the last glaciation, the age of lake sediments, and to calibrate other dating methods.

*Limitations.*

- Only possible where there are **marked seasons, ice-fed lakes with seasonal melting**; it **cannot be used in the tropics** or in lakes that did not develop clear summer and winter layers.
- **Missing or disturbed varves**: erosion, turbidity currents, floods or burrowing animals can **remove, double or blur layers**, and one season may produce **more than one couplet**, which gives errors in the count.
- Matching of varves between lakes is difficult, and the sequence is **floating** (not tied to the present) unless linked to a dated layer; it only covers the **last 15 000 years or so**; and it needs exposures or cores that are complete.
- It gives only the **local** age of the deposit and not an absolute age for older strata.
